## Chapter 5: The Integral Calculus Proper
<details>
<summary>Algebraic Trickery (Rational Functions)</summary>
<details>
<summary>Antiderivative of $\frac{1}{x}$</summary>
$$
\int \frac{1}{x}\ dx = \ln{|x|} + C
$$
</details>
<details>
<summary>Antiderivative of $sec{(x)}$ and $csc{(x)}$</summary>
$$
\begin{align}
\int \sec{(x)}\ dx &= \ln{|\sec{(x)} + \tan{(x)}|} + C \\
\int \csc{(x)}\ dx &= -\ln{|\csc{(x)} + \cot{(x)}|} + C
\end{align}
$$
</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary>Trigonometric Trickery (Part 1)</summary>
<details>
<summary>Pythagorean identities</summary>
$$
\begin{align}
\sin^2{x} + \cos^2{x} &= 1 \\
\sec^2{x} - \tan^2{x} &= 1
\end{align}
$$
</details>
<details>
<summary>Double-angle identities</summary>
$$
\begin{align}
\cos{(2x)} &= \cos^2{x} - \sin^2{x} \\
\sin{(2x)} &= 2\sin{x}\cos{x}
\end{align}
$$
</details>
</details>
<details>
<summary>Trigonometric Trickery (Part 2)</summary>
<details>
<summary>Trigonometric substitution</summary>
We replace $x$ with a trigonometric function to complete the square and thus get rid of the square root. The Pythagorean identities are the squaremakers.

- For $\sqrt{\text{constant} - \text{square}}$, we use: $\sin^2{\theta} + \cos^2{\theta} = 1$. For example, with $\sqrt{9-x^2}$ our substitution is $x = 3\sin{\theta}$ which transforms the expression into $\sqrt{(3\cos{\theta})^2}$.
- For $\sqrt{\text{square} + \text{constant}}$, we use: $\sec^2{\theta} - \tan^2{\theta} = 1$. For example, with $\sqrt{x^2+16}$ our substitution is $x = 4\tan{\theta}$ which transforms the expression into $\sqrt{(4\sec{\theta})^2}$.
- For $\sqrt{\text{square} - \text{constant}}$, we use: $\sec^2{\theta} - \tan^2{\theta} = 1$. For example, with $\sqrt{x^2-3}$ our substitution is $x = \sqrt{3}\sec{\theta}$ which transforms the expression into $\sqrt{(\sqrt{3}\tan{\theta})^2}$.

</details>
